The configuration a Database is built from, the database object itself,
and the operations that apply to the whole database: waiting for a write
to become durable, inspecting the writer, and closing it.

DatabaseConfig(; dbname, user, host="localhost", port=5432, password=nothing,
                 sslmode="prefer", connect_timeout=10, readpoolsize=8,
                 max_batch=1, failure=:isolate, retries=nothing, retry_time=nothing,
                 retry_delay=0.1, retry_delay_max=5.0, on_error=nothing,
                 conninfo=nothing)
DatabaseConfig(url::AbstractString; kwargs...)

The parameters AirDB uses to reach a PostgreSQL database and to decide how it
behaves. The server is the user’s to configure and manage; AirDB only connects.

dbname and user are required unless conninfo is given. conninfo, when
set, is a libpq connection string or URI used verbatim (as built by the
url method), and the structured fields are ignored.

readpoolsize — how many read connections to keep in the pool.

max_batch — how many committed updates the pipeline accumulates before
flushing. 1 (the default) writes every commit as soon as it arrives.

failure — what to do when an operation fails permanently:

:isolate (the default) — quarantine the failing batch, record it (see


write_failures), and keep serving unrelated reads and writes.

:abort — the write pipeline stops and every database operation raises.

:retry — a compatibility alias for the isolated retry path.
:isolate and :retry retry within the budget before quarantining; :abort
gives up immediately.

retries / retry_time — the retry budget: at most this many attempts, or at
most this many seconds. If both are given, whichever runs out first wins; if
neither is given under :isolate/:retry, a small default is used.

retry_delay / retry_delay_max — the delay before the first retry and its
ceiling; the delay doubles after each failed attempt up to the ceiling.

on_error — a hook on_error(db, err) called on every database error, before
the policy is applied. It may return :retry or :abort to override the
policy, an Integer to retry at most that many more times, a Real to retry
for that many seconds, or nothing to use the configured policy. It can read


pending_writes on db to see the unsaved updates.

encoder_tasks — how many tasks encode committed batches (the form JSON,
extern serialization, stream snapshots). Encoding happens after commit and in
parallel with database writes; the default is max(1, min(4, nthreads()-1)).

max_pending — the most committed-but-unwritten batches allowed before a
committing thread waits. This bounds the writer’s lag; the default is 256.

Database

A configured connection to a PostgreSQL database, plus the machinery AirDB keeps
around it: a pool of read connections, a weak cache of live VolatileForms, an
intake actor, an encoder pool, and a single ordered writer task that persists
committed updates in global commit order.

Create one with 

create_database (to initialize a new database) or


open_database (to open an existing one).

create_database(config::DatabaseConfig; overwrite::Bool=false) -> Database

Initializes a new AirDB database in the PostgreSQL instance described by
config — creating the form_history, form_current, and airdb_meta tables
and starting a Database for it. The server itself is the user’s to provide and
manage.

With overwrite=true the three AirDB tables are dropped and recreated first.

open_database(config::DatabaseConfig) -> Database

Opens an AirDB database that already exists in the PostgreSQL instance described
by config. Raises if the AirDB schema is missing (use 

create_database
to make one).

MemoryDatabase() -> MemoryDatabase

A fake, in-memory 

Database for testing without PostgreSQL. It behaves
like a real database — forms persist across commits, named forms work, sync
blocks — but keeps everything in memory, saves nothing, and keeps no history.

sync(db::Database)

Blocks until every update sent to db before this call has been written to the
database. The pipeline’s writer is sequential, so once it has passed the sync
barrier every earlier write is durable.

Under :isolate, a quarantined batch does not make sync raise (see


write_failures); under :abort, the recorded DatabaseError is
raised.

status(db::Database) -> (npending, error)

The number of updates queued for the writer but not yet written, and the last
error the writer saw (or nothing). The intake is asynchronous, so a commit
that has just returned may not be counted yet; 

sync waits for it.

close(sf::StreamForm)

Closes the stream: a later put! raises Air.StreamClosed, and a take
drains what remains and then raises it too. Idempotent; staged inside a
transaction.close(db::Database)

Flushes any queued writes and closes every connection the database holds. Further
operations raise.

DatabaseError(cause, failed_writes)

Raised, or recorded on a Database, when a database operation fails under the
:abort policy. cause is the underlying exception and failed_writes holds the
updates that could not be saved.

FormNotFound(id)

Raised when a form’s id is not present in the database.

The type-sensitive equivalence relation and the hash that agrees with
it. See 

Equivalence.

isequiv(a::Form, b::Form) -> Bool

Whether two forms are equivalent: equal in both value and type, with object
identity for anything mutable.

A FormScalar is equivalent to another only when the leaves have the same type
and an equal value (NaN is equivalent to itself, and -0.0 to 0.0). Thus
Form(5) == Form(5.0) but !isequiv(Form(5), Form(5.0)), and a BigInt(5) is
not equivalent to an Int64(5). A FormContainer is equivalent when its
sequences match position by position and its maps have the same keys with
equivalent values.

A VolatileForm, ActorForm, PromiseForm, StreamForm, or mutable extern is
equivalent only to the same object. An immutable extern is equivalent only to
itself unless its type registered equal/hash functions with


register_extern; a DelayForm is equivalent when its type and
serialization form are equivalent.

Use 

equivhash for a hash that agrees with this relation.

equivhash(x::Form, h::UInt = zero(UInt)) -> UInt

A hash consistent with 

isequiv: equivalent forms hash equally. It is
not Base.hash — numeric leaves hash by type and value, so Form(5) and
Form(5.0) differ; a signed zero hashes as 0.0; every NaN hashes to one value;
and a mutable form hashes by object identity.

h is a seed, so equivhash composes like Base.hash.

Host-level values: registration, construction, calls, reservations, and
the form that wraps them. See


Extern types.

AbstractAirExtern

The supertype of a host-level value a form can hold without being JSON itself —
a socket, a promise, a configuration handle, a cached value. A form stores one
inside a 

FormExtern; its operations, constructors, and optional
serialization are declared with 

register_extern.

FormExtern(handle)

A form holding a host-level 

AbstractAirExtern: an object whose
operations are defined by its registered type and whose data lives in an
ExternHandle. Build one with construct; use 

value to get the
data back.

DeadExtern(type)

The data of a 

FormExtern whose object could not be stored: it was
unnamed, or its type declared no serialization. A dead extern carries only the
registered type name and raises whenever it is used.

ExternAPI

A handle to an extern’s interface. A type-level API (from
get_extern_API(name)) carries no data and is used with 

construct. A
value-level API (from get_extern_API(fe) for immutable types, or handed to a


reserve/

reserve_read function) carries the data and is used with
call.

ExternError

Raised when an extern is used incorrectly: an unregistered type or operation, an
API requested for a mutable extern without a reservation, a dead extern touched,
or a resource that cannot be loaded.

ExternPromise

The promise returned by 

reserve. p[] waits for the reservation and
yields its result, re-raising any error the function raised.

register_extern(name, ::Type{T}; read_only, read_edit, constructors,
                immutable = false, serialize = nothing, deserialize = nothing)

Register an extern data type T under name. read_only and read_edit are
PDicts of keyword operators to (data, args) -> Form functions; constructors
is a PDict of keyword operators to (args) -> data functions. A read-edit
operation may mutate the data and therefore requires a 

reserve; an
immutable type must declare none, and its API is available to any thread.

serialize(data, io) writes the data and deserialize(io) reads it back. A type
with both is database-storable: a form may hold a named extern of that type, and
the bytes live in the resources table. A type with neither is never stored — a
form that holds one is written as a dead-extern marker.

An immutable type may also declare equal(a, b) -> Bool and
hash(data, seed::UInt) -> UInt (both, or neither). They give the type value
semantics in 

isequiv/

equivhash; without them, two externs
are equivalent only when they wrap the same live handle. A mutable type is
always identity-equivalent and may not declare them.register_extern(:config, ConfigData;
    read_only = PDict(Symbol(":version") => (d, args) -> Form(d.version)),
    read_edit = PDict(Symbol(":bump") => (d, args) -> (d.version += 1; Form(d.version))),
    constructors = PDict(Symbol(":new") => args -> ConfigData(1)),
    immutable = false,
    serialize = (d, io) -> print(io, d.version),
    deserialize = io -> ConfigData(parse(Int, read(io, String))))

get_extern_API(name::Symbol) -> ExternAPI

The type-level API for the extern type registered under name, used with


construct.get_extern_API(fe::FormExtern) -> ExternAPI

The API for an immutable extern, usable from any thread. A mutable extern raises:
it must be 

reserved (or 

reserve_read) first.

construct(api::ExternAPI, ctor::Form, args::Form; id = nothing) -> FormExtern

Run the constructor named by ctor (a keyword form) with args, and wrap the
returned data in a 

FormExtern. id, if given, is the keyword under
which the extern is stored; it must be unique among live externs.

call(api::ExternAPI, op::Form, args::Form) -> Form

Run the operation named by op (a keyword form) on the extern’s data with
args. Through a read-only API only read-only operations are available; through
an API handed out by 

reserve the read-edit operations are too.

reserve(f, resources...) -> ExternPromise

Run f with editable APIs for each resource on a spawned task, which first takes
their write locks in sorted (type, id) order. Returns a promise; wait on it
with p[] for f’s value.

Inside a transaction the function is not run until the transaction commits (and
is discarded if it retries), and the reservation counts as a read: f’s
resources’ versions must be unchanged at commit. Reading the promise inside that
same transaction before it completes raises.p = reserve(r1) do api
    api.call(Form(Symbol(":bump")), form())
end
p[]          # the result

reserve_read(f, resources...) -> value

Run f with read-only APIs for each resource, taking their read locks in sorted
(type, id) order first. Runs on the caller’s task and returns f’s value.
Inside a transaction the versions are read, so a concurrent read-edit forces the
transaction to retry. This is the ordinary way to call read-only operations.reserve_read(r1, r2) do api1, api2
    api1.call(Form(Symbol(":version")), form())
end

The records a quarantined batch leaves behind, the queries that inspect
them, and the calls that clear or retry one. See


Inspecting failures.

FailedItem

One object that a quarantined batch could not save: its kind
(:form, :actor, :promise, :stream, :extern, or :name), its id
(a UUID, a (type, id) pair, or a name), the live object when one is known,
and the pending write that failed.

FailureRecord

One quarantined batch: the batch’s sequence number, the database error, when it
happened, and the 

FailedItems it contained.

ReadFailure

A read that failed and was not retried successfully: the error, when it
happened, the operation (:load, :metadata, :name, :read, ...), and the
object id when the read was for one.

FailedObjectError(id, record)

Raised when an object whose database write was quarantined is loaded. The live
in-memory object remains readable; reloading it would silently return the older
row, so it raises instead. See 

write_failures and


clear_write_failure!.

failed(db, id) -> Bool

Whether id currently has an unsaved (quarantined) write. A live in-memory
object is still readable; loading it raises 

FailedObjectError.

clear_write_failure!(db, id; retry = false) -> Bool

Acknowledge and remove the quarantined writes for id. With retry = true,
also re-stage the object’s current in-memory value for another write (a
form’s value and metadata, an actor’s value, a stream’s snapshot, an extern’s
bytes, the current name mapping, or a promise’s outcome). Returns whether
anything was cleared.

clear_write_failures!(db) -> Nothing

Acknowledge and remove every quarantined write.

clear_read_failures!(db) -> Nothing

Clear the read-failure history.

pending_writes(db::Database)

The updates the writer has not yet saved — form writes, actor values, queued
stream snapshots, resource bytes, promise rows and settlements, names, and
metadata-only edits — plus any writes that were quarantined by the failure
policy. This is meant for use inside an on_error hook, where the writer is
between attempts and its queue is the work that a successful retry would save.
If the writer has already been poisoned (:abort), the writes from the failed
batch are returned instead.

The abstract supertype of every form: 

FormScalar (a bare leaf),

A form holding just a leaf (see

Nothing, or one of the numeric tower’s value types. Form(x) for a leaf x

A form holding a sequence of positional values (seq) and a map of symbol-keyed

FormLeaf

The scalar values a form can hold: String, Symbol, Bool, Nothing, and
the numeric tower wherever it is a value type —
Int64, BigInt, Float64, BigFloat, Rational{Int64},
Rational{BigInt}, ComplexF64 and Complex{BigFloat}. A 

FormScalar
wraps one; a

types are converted to one of these where the conversion is exact; see

FormValue

What a

Form or a

Build a container from its arguments: the positional arguments become the

x as a form: a form is returned as it is, a leaf becomes a

value(fs::FormScalar)
value(fe::FormExtern)

The leaf a scalar form wraps, or the data an extern form wraps (loading it from

any 

Form, FormLeaf, Bool, Symbol, String, Char, Integer,

a Complex whose parts are exactly Float64 or exactly BigFloat (so

The sweep that reclaims rows nothing references any more, and its
statistics.

gc!(db; dry_run = false, batch = 1000) -> GCStats

Sweeps unreachable database objects. The roots are the named forms (form_name)
and every live in-memory object (VolatileForm, ActorForm, PromiseForm, and
extern handle), so an object referenced only from a live handle survives. The
sweep removes unreachable rows from form_current, form_actor_current,
form_promise, and resources, and deletes the history rows of the swept
objects; live objects keep their full history.

The sweep runs as one job on the database’s writer task, so it sees a
consistent snapshot and blocks only writes (reads continue). Object loading is
serialized with it, so a row cannot be swept while it is being loaded. Names are
never removed here; use 

delete_name! to release one.

dry_run = true reports what would be swept without deleting anything.

MemoryDatabase implements the same sweep over its in-memory stores.

GCStats

What a 

gc! sweep scanned and removed, per object kind, and how long it
took.

The textual form used for storage and interchange. See


The JSON format.

to_JSON(f::Form) -> String

The form as a JSON string. A container is written as the two-element list
[seq, map], so the format is self-describing: from_JSON reads a list as a
container (or an extern — see below). A scalar form is written as its bare leaf.

A String and a Symbol are both written as JSON strings, with the first
character inside the quotes saying which: ' for a string and : for a symbol.
A Float64 is a plain number, always with a decimal point or an exponent so that
it reads back as a float rather than as an integer. Values outside JSON’s number
model are marked strings: a non-finite Float64 — Inf, -Inf, or NaN — is
"#inf", "#-inf", or "#nan", a BigInt is "#big:<digits>", a
Rational is "#rat:<num>/<den>" or "#bigrat:<num>/<den>", and a BigFloat
is "#bigfloat:<precision>:<digits>" (with its precision in bits). The #
marker cannot be confused with a string ('), a symbol (:), or a link (@).
A complex number has no JSON equivalent and is written as
{"re": …, "im": …}, always, even when its imaginary part is zero; a
Complex{BigFloat} writes its parts as BigFloats.
A 

VolatileForm is written as the string
"@<uuid>"; it is never expanded, so cyclic links are safe to write. A


FormExtern is written as the object {"extern": "<type>", "id": "<id>"} — or {"extern": "<type>"} when it is dead — and its bytes live in the
resources table. An 

ActorForm, 

PromiseForm, and


StreamForm are written as the links "!<uuid>", "~<uuid>", and
"&<uuid>"; a promise is a link whether it is pending, delivered, or failed.to_JSON(vf::VolatileForm) -> String

The volatile form’s link text, "@<uuid>" (without the surrounding JSON quotes).

from_JSON(s::AbstractString) -> Form
from_JSON(resolve::Function, s::AbstractString) -> Form
from_JSON(db::Database, s::AbstractString) -> Form

a list [seq, map]; a bare object is accepted as a form with only a map, and a

A form may link to a

a link requires a database, so either pass one, or pass a function that turns a
UUID into the value the link should yield. Reading a form that contains a link
without a resolver is an error.

An object with the plain key extern is a

looked up in the registry (see

from the resources table lazily. An object with no id is a dead extern; an

Stable names for forms, and the alias table that resolves them.

named_form(db::Database, name; create = false, value = nothing)

Look up the form registered under name, which may be a Symbol or a String.
create controls what happens when the name is not found:

create = false (the default) — raise if no form is registered under name;

create = true — create a new named form and return it, raising if the name is
already in use;

create = nothing — never raise; return nothing when the name is not found.

value is the new form’s initial value, used only when a form is created. It is
converted with 

to_form, so a 

Form is used as-is, a number
becomes a 

FormScalar, a collection becomes a container, and leaving it
out gives an empty container; or it may be an existing 

VolatileForm, in
which case no new form is made and the name is pointed at the given one.

Creating is transactional: it joins the caller’s transaction if there is one, and
otherwise runs in a transaction of its own.

root = named_form(db, "root"; create = true, value = form(version = 1))
named_form(db, "root")                 # the same form
named_form(db, :root)                  # Symbol and String agree
named_form(db, "root"; create = true)  # ERROR: already in use
named_form(db, "other"; create = nothing)   # nothing

name_form!(db::Database, name, vf::VolatileForm) -> VolatileForm

Registers vf under name, overwriting any form already registered under it.
Transactional, like 

named_form.

named_forms(db::Database) -> PDict{String,VolatileForm}

The whole name table as it currently stands. The PDict is immutable, so it is
safe to share and to keep; each value is a (possibly not-yet-loaded)


VolatileForm. Inside a transaction this registers a read of the table.

delete_name!(db::Database, name)

Removes the alias name (a Symbol or a String). The form itself is untouched;
once nothing else refers to it, 

gc! may collect it. Transactional, like


name_form!.

Forms are navigated with a path of keys. The same indexing works on any form,
and a VolatileForm met along the way is transparent — its value is used in its
place — which makes a tree of forms read like a single nested value.

An Integer is a sequence position; a Symbol is a map key.

A vector key (or :, meaning every key) fans out, building a new form
over the selection.

A value read out of a container is wrapped back into a form, so indexing always
yields a form: a leaf comes back as a FormScalar, which value unwraps. The
value at the final key is returned as it is, so a final VolatileForm
comes back whole rather than expanded.

f = form(10, 20, 30, a = form(x = 1, y = 2), b = form(x = 3))

f[1]              # Form(10)
value(f[1])       # 10
f[:a]             # Form(x=1, y=2)
value(f[:a, :x])  # 1   — same as value(f[:a][:x])

A VolatileForm is transparent when you index through it, but returned whole
when it is the final value:a = VolatileForm(db, x = 0)
b = VolatileForm(db, x = 1)
fv = form(a = a, b = b)

fv[:a]            # the VolatileForm itself
value(fv[:a, :x]) # 0    — fv[:a] was dereferenced to reach :x
value(fv[:a][:x]) # 0

A vector key builds a form over the selection. Because reading extracts data,
volatiles are eliminated from whatever it builds — a VolatileForm in the result
is replaced by its value.f[[:a, :b], :x]        # Form(a=1, b=3)
f[[:a, :b], [:x]]      # Form(a=(x=1), b=(x=3)) — a nested level per vector
f[2:3]                 # Form(20, 30) — a range is a vector key, so it fans out

A range over the sequence’s own collection gives the subsequence, as a sequence
rather than a plain Vector, so it can be used as a container’s sequence:f.seq[2:3]             # the subsequence holding 20 and 30

With volatiles in the tree:g = form(a = VolatileForm(db, x = 0), b = VolatileForm(db, x = 1))

g[[:a, :b], :x]        # Form(a=0, b=1)          — the volatiles are eliminated
g[[:a, :b], [:x]]      # Form(a=(x=0), b=(x=1))

: selects every sequence position and every map key:h = form(form(x = 10), form(x = 20), a = form(x = 30))
h[:, :x]               # Form(10, 20, a=30)

A missing key raises. get supplies a default for a missing final key; a
missing intermediate key still raises.f[:z]                          # ERROR: KeyError: key :z not found
get(f, :z, :none)              # :none
get(f, :a, :z, :none)          # :none   — :a exists, :z does not
get(f, :z, :x, :none)          # ERROR: KeyError — the intermediate :z is missing

There are two ways to update. A functional update builds a new form and
leaves the original untouched. A transactional update writes through the
VolatileForms on the path, changing their values in place; it must run inside
a transaction. The transaction rule itself is covered in


Transactions; this page is about the update
operations.

setindex builds a new form and never writes a volatile. A volatile on the
update path is therefore eliminated (replaced by its plain, updated value);
volatiles off the path are kept as links.f = form(10, 20, a = form(x = 1, y = 2), b = form(x = 3))

setindex(f, 99, :a, :x)        # Form(10, 20, a=(x=99, y=2), b=(x=3))
setindex(f, 5, 1)              # Form(5, 20, a=..., b=...)
setindex(f, 42, :c)            # adds a new key
setindex(f, 4, 3)              # appends: Form(10, 20, 4, a=..., b=...)g = form(a = VolatileForm(db, x = 0), b = VolatileForm(db, x = 1))
r = setindex(g, 99, :a, :x)
r[:a]                          # Form(x=99) — a plain container; the volatile is gone
r[:b] === g[:b]                # true       — the off-path volatile is kept

A fan-out setindex returns a form over the selection:setindex(f, 99, [:a, :b], :x)  # Form(a=(x=99, y=2), b=(x=99))

An integer index equal to one past the end of the sequence appends:setindex(form(1, 2, 3), 4, 4)  # Form(1, 2, 3, 4)
setindex(form(1, 2, 3), 9, 5)  # ERROR: BoundsError

setindex! walks the path and writes the deepest VolatileForm on it — the
last volatile among the values along the path, including the final one. It
rebuilds that volatile along the keys below it. If no value on the path is a
volatile, it raises, because an ordinary form cannot be mutated.@tx g[:a, :x] = 5              # writes the volatile g[:a]; reads g

Because it writes a volatile, setindex! must run inside a transaction. Setting
the final key sets the final volatile’s value:@tx g[:a] = form(x = 42)       # sets the value of the volatile at :a

A fan-out writes each branch’s target:@tx g[[:a, :b], :x] = 9        # writes both volatiles

An integer one past the end of a sequence appends:seq = VolatileForm(db, 1, 2)
@tx seq[3] = 3                 # seq[] == Form(1, 2, 3)

Writes are not local

setindex! writes the deepest volatile, which may be shared with other
structures, so the change is visible everywhere that volatile is reachable. This
is the intended model — volatiles are identity objects — but it means the effect
of g[:a, 1] = x is not always obvious from the call site.

map returns a form with the same keys, every immediate value replaced by
fn(value). A VolatileForm value is handed to fn as the VolatileForm
object, so the function decides whether to keep or drop it. If the form itself is
a VolatileForm, the function is applied to its value; if it is a FormScalar,
it is applied to the leaf.f = form(10, 20, a = form(x = 1), b = 3)

map(x -> x * 2, form(1, 2, a = 3))     # Form(2, 4, a=6)
map(x -> x + 1, Form(5))               # Form(6)
map(identity, g)                       # same keys; the volatiles are passed through
map(v -> v isa VolatileForm ? v[] : v, g)    # ... or expanded, if you prefer

The functional verbs push, pop, and delete likewise operate on a
VolatileForm’s value and return a new form; they never write the volatile.g = form(1, 2, 3)
push(g, 4)          # Form(1, 2, 3, 4)
pop(g)              # Form(1, 2)
delete(g, 2)        # Form(1, 3) — items shift down; no blanks

Beyond get/setindex, a form is operated on with the usual functional verbs.
Each value handed to a function is passed as a form.f = form(10, 20, a = form(x = 1), b = 3)
vf = VolatileForm(db, n = 0)

update(f, v -> value(v) + 1, :a, :x)   # read-modify-write: Form(10, 20, a=(x=2), b=3)
update!(vf, v -> value(v) + 1, :n)     # ... transactional: deepest volatile, like setindex!

merge(form(a = 1), form(b = 2))        # Form(a=1, b=2)
merge(form(a = 1), form(a = 9))        # Form(a=9) — the later form wins
merge_with((x, y) -> value(x) + value(y), form(a = 1), form(a = 2))   # Form(a=3)

haskey(f, :a, :x)                      # true — haskey takes a path
select_keys(f, [:b, :a])               # Form(a=(x=1), b=3); missing keys are skipped

filter(v -> v isa FormScalar && value(v) isa Int64, form(1, "s", a = 2))  # Form(1, a=2)
map_values(v -> value(v) + 1, form(1, a = 2))   # Form(2, a=3)
map_keys(k -> Symbol("k_", k), form(a = 1))     # Form(k_a=1)
deep_map(v -> v isa FormScalar && value(v) isa Int64 ? Form(value(v) + 1) : v,
         form(1, a = 2))                       # Form(2, a=3): every leaf, bottom-up

to_vector(form(1, 2, 3))   # [1, 2, 3]
to_dict(form(a = 1))       # Dict(:a => 1)

update and the other verbs without a ! are purely functional; update!
writes the deepest VolatileForm on the path and raises if there is none — the
same rule as setindex! — so it must run inside a transaction.

A Form is an immutable, nested, JSON-able value. Every node in a form tree is
a form:

a FormScalar holds a single leaf;

a FormContainer holds a sequence of positional values and a map of
symbol-keyed ones;

a VolatileForm (see 

Volatile forms) holds a form
that persists itself in a database;

a FormExtern (see 

Extern types) holds
a host-level value that is not JSON itself; and

ActorForm, PromiseForm, StreamForm, and DelayForm
(see 

Actors, 

Promises,


Streams, and 

Delays) hold live Air
objects.

This page is about the plain values: scalars and containers.

A leaf on its own is a form:using AirDB

Form("abc")             # Form("abc")
Form(5)                 # Form(5)
Form(nothing)           # Form(nothing)
value(Form("abc"))      # "abc" — unwrap a scalar form to its leaf

The leaves a form can hold are String, Symbol, Bool, Nothing, and the
numeric tower’s value types: Int64, BigInt, Float64, BigFloat,
Rational{Int64}, Rational{BigInt}, ComplexF64 and Complex{BigFloat}. A
wider or narrower scalar is converted where the conversion cannot lose
information:Form(Int32(7))          # Form(7) — an Int64
Form(Int128(2)^70)      # a BigInt: it does not fit in an Int64
Form('x')               # Form("x")
Form(1 + 2im)           # Form(1.0 + 2.0im)
Form(true)              # Form(true) — Bool stays Bool
Form(1 // 3)            # Form(1//3) — a Rational{Int64}
Form(big"1.5")          # a BigFloat, at its own precision

Each of these leaf types survives a JSON round trip as the same Julia type and
value; a BigFloat keeps its precision. A value that fits no exact leaf —
Complex(1//3, 0), say — raises rather than rounding. The one lossy conversion
is an Irrational constant (π, ℯ), which becomes a Float64.
is_form_representable(x) answers whether to_form(x) will succeed, without
raising, so a caller can check first:is_form_representable(1 // 3)             # true
is_form_representable(complex(1 // 3, 0)) # false
is_form_representable([1, 2])             # true, recursively

form(...) builds a container: its positional arguments become the sequence and
its keyword arguments the map.f = form("widget", 1, 2.5, meta = form(name = "abc"))
f                       # Form("widget", 1, 2.5, meta=(name="abc"))

Every value must be a leaf or another form. A Vector or Dict argument
becomes a nested container, so ordinary Julia collections nest naturally:form([1, 2, 3])         # Form((1, 2, 3))
form(Dict(:a => 1))     # Form((a=1))

Form vs. form

Form(x) builds a scalar form from one leaf, and Form(seq, map) builds a
container from prepared collections. form(...) is the general builder, and
to_form converts any value to a form.

How a container is stored

A container’s sequence and map are held in a small, flat, copy-on-write form
while they are small — which is the common case — and promoted to Air’s
persistent structure above a threshold. Every update copies, so a form shared
between two values is never changed under either of them; you never need to know
which representation is in use. (PDict and PVector are Air’s persistent map
and vector types.)

A form is a collection, so it iterates in one canonical order — every sequence
position, then every map key sorted — and supports the usual tools.f = form(10, 20, a = 30)

length(f)          # 3
isempty(f)         # false
keys(f)            # 1, 2, :a
values(f)          # iterates Form(10), Form(20), Form(30)
pairs(f)           # iterates 1 => Form(10), 2 => Form(20), :a => Form(30)

for (k, v) in f
    # iterates the pairs, in the canonical order
end

collect(f)         # Any[1 => Form(10), 2 => Form(20), :a => Form(30)]
Dict(collect(f))   # a Dict of the same pairs
first(f)           # 1 => Form(10)
last(f)            # :a => Form(30)

copy(f) === f      # true — forms are immutable
empty(f)           # Form() — the empty container

A scalar form has no elements: length(Form(5)) == 0.

A symbol that begins with a colon is a keyword, and one that begins with a
question mark is a wildcard. They are ordinary leaves with distinct text, so
a keyword and a wildcard are never equal to each other or to a plain symbol.

iswildcard(Form(Symbol("?abc"))) # true
iskeyword(Form(:abc))            # false — a plain symbol
iswildcard(Form(Symbol(":abc"))) # false

Form(Symbol(":abc"))             # not equal to Form(Symbol("?abc")) or Form(:abc)

A PostgreSQL-backed persistence layer built on


Air.jl’s software transactional memory.

AirDB keeps shared application state in memory as ordinary Julia values and
writes every committed change to PostgreSQL automatically, in transaction order,
without locks in your own code. It is aimed at asynchronous, multithreaded
servers whose threads share data and whose write order matters.

Air provides three building blocks:

a Volatile, a Ref-like cell that may only be written inside a
transaction and is guaranteed constant for the duration of one;

an Actor, a worker with its own task and message queue, which runs sent
functions one at a time; and

transactions (@tx / tx), which make a group of reads, writes, and sends
take effect all at once or not at all, re-running the body if another thread
interferes.

AirDB builds on those:

Form — an immutable, JSON-able nested value: the type that gets stored.
Forms are introduced in 

Form values.

VolatileForm — a form with a stable UUID that writes itself to the
database when the transaction that changed it commits. See


Volatile forms.

Database — the connection, the write pipeline, the read pool, and a
cache of live forms. See 

Opening a database.

Live forms and externs — forms backed by an Air actor, promise, delay, or
stream, and forms holding host-level values such as sockets or configuration
handles. These are introduced later, in

Extern types.

One ordered writer, many readers

Every Database owns one ordered writer: committed updates are written in
Air’s commit order, so the database never sees two writers race. Reads go
through a separate pool of connections and never wait on the writer. The


Concurrency page covers the details.

The rest of this book explains each piece; here is the whole shape of a small
program:using AirDB
using Air            # for @tx and the Air types

cfg = DatabaseConfig(; host = "localhost", dbname = "airdb_test",
                       user = "airdb", password = "airdb")
db = create_database(cfg; overwrite = true)   # create the tables and connect

widget = VolatileForm(db, "widget", n = 1)    # a form, persisted on commit
value(widget[:n])                             # 1

@tx widget[:n] = 42                           # a transaction: stage the change
AirDB.sync(db)                                # wait until the writer has saved it
value(widget[:n])                             # 42

The value now lives both in memory and in PostgreSQL. Another process, or a
later session, can read it by its UUID:id = widget.id
close(db)
db = open_database(cfg)
r = get_form(db, id)      # a fresh handle; the body is read lazily
value(r[:n])              # 42

The write rule (@tx), sync, and lazy loading are explained in

next pages build this example up from the beginning.

PDict — Air’s persistent (immutable) dictionary; updating one copies it.

Volatile — Air’s transactional Ref-like cell: readable at any time,
writable only inside a transaction.

uses these.

@tx / tx — Air’s transaction macro and function. Writes are made inside
them; see

reserve_read takes the read locks of every resource, in sorted (type, id)
order (which prevents deadlock), runs the function on the caller’s task, and
returns its value. Read-only operations run concurrently with one another, and
never during a read-edit.

positions depend on their names, not the order you named them. A read-edit of a

A form holds leaves and other forms — everything JSON can say. A running program
also holds things JSON cannot: a socket, a promise, a configuration handle.
These are extern types. A provider defines the type, its operations in
Julia, and how (and whether) it is stored; AirDB supplies the form wrapper, the
concurrency, and the database storage.

This page covers declaring and constructing an extern type. Calling its
operations and reserving it are in


Calling and reservations; storing it is in


Storage and dead externs.

An extern’s data is any type that subclasses AbstractAirExtern. Its interface
is registered once, at startup:using AirDB, Air

mutable struct Counter <: AbstractAirExtern
    n::Int
end

register_extern(:counter, Counter;
    read_only = PDict(
        Symbol(":get") => (d, args) -> Form(d.n)),
    read_edit = PDict(
        Symbol(":bump") => (d, args) -> (d.n += 1; Form(d.n))),
    constructors = PDict(
        Symbol(":new") => args -> Counter(Int(value(args)))),
    serialize = (d, io) -> print(io, d.n),
    deserialize = io -> Counter(parse(Int, read(io, String))))

read_only and read_edit are PDicts from keyword operation names to
(data, args) -> Form functions. Every operation is classified when it is
defined: a read-edit operation mutates the data and therefore needs a write
lock, while read-only operations may run concurrently.

constructors are keyword-named (args) -> data functions; they produce the
object’s data from an argument form.

immutable = true declares that the data never changes: no read-edit
operations are allowed, and the API is available to every thread at any time.

serialize/deserialize are both present or both absent. With them, a named
extern can be stored in the database; without them it is never stored.

equal = (a, b) -> Bool and hash = (data, seed) -> UInt (both, or neither)
are optional for an immutable type. They give the extern value semantics
in 

isequiv/equivhash. Without them — and for
every mutable extern — two externs are equivalent only when they wrap the same
live handle.

Operation and constructor names are keywords, as in Form(Symbol(":get")).

constructor and returns a FormExtern:c = construct(get_extern_API(:counter), Form(Symbol(":new")), Form(3))

different type, or a type under a second name, raises ExternError.

A StreamForm is a FIFO of forms backed by an Air Stream{Form}. It is like a
promise that can be written and read repeatedly: put! appends, take removes

bounded, can time out, and can be closed, and its queued contents are persisted.using AirDB

sf = StreamForm(db; maxsize = 3)
put!(sf, form(id = 1))
put!(sf, form(id = 2))

length(sf)        # 2
snapshot(sf)      # Form[Form(id=1), Form(id=2)] — a copy; nothing is removed
take(sf)          # Form(id=1)
take(sf)          # Form(id=2)

maxsize bounds how many forms may wait: nothing (the default) leaves the
stream unbounded, so put! never waits. A write to a full stream waits for a
read to make room. Both reads and writes accept timeout (in seconds) and a
cancellation token, as Air’s take and put! do:sf = StreamForm(db; maxsize = 1)
put!(sf, 1)
put!(sf, 2; timeout = 0.05)   # ERROR: Air.ReaderTimeout

take(sf)                       # 1 — the timeout freed nothing
take(sf; timeout = 0.05)       # ERROR: Air.ReaderTimeout (now empty)

take drains the values that remain and then raises it too.put!(sf, 7); close(sf)

take(sf)      # ERROR: Air.StreamClosed

blocking.

transaction happens only if the transaction commits, the transaction that staged
it sees its own writes and reads, and a concurrent change makes the attempt
retry. A blocking operation on a stream created in the current transaction
raises Air.StreamDeadlock — no other task can reach it until the commit — and
a stream first loaded in the transaction is treated the same way. AirDB sends
the stream’s updated contents to the database writer only if the transaction
commits. See

AirDB is built for many threads sharing data. The model is simple: many readers
and writers, one ordered writer.

Reads go through a pool of connections and never wait on the writer. A commit
hands its batch to an intake actor and returns; a pool of encoder tasks turns
committed batches into their JSON payloads, extern bytes, and stream snapshots;
one writer task owns the PostgreSQL connection and writes prepared batches in
commit order. So the database sees transactions in exactly the order they were
enqueued — no deadlocks, no row-level lock contention, no two writers racing —
while a slow form or extern serialization no longer holds up the commit path or
the writer’s intake.counter = VolatileForm(db, n = 0)
AirDB.sync(db)

@sync for _ in 1:50
    Threads.@spawn tx(() -> (counter[:n] = value(counter[:n]) + 1))
end
AirDB.sync(db)

value(counter[:n])                 # 50 — every increment committed exactly once

max_pending bounds how far the writer may lag: a committing thread waits only
when that many committed batches are still unwritten. encoder_tasks controls
the encoding pool (the default is max(1, min(4, nthreads()-1))).

Under contention Air re-runs transactions that lose a race, so the final value
is correct even though the bodies run more than once. The history reflects only

A connection to PostgreSQL can fail at any time — a dropped socket, a restart, a
network blip — and a particular row can be impossible to write. AirDB lets you
choose what a permanent failure does with failure on the DatabaseConfig:
:isolate (the default), :abort, or :retry.

Retries are separate from the terminal action. :isolate and :retry both retry
a failing operation while a budget lasts (reconnecting first); when the
budget is spent, they quarantine the batch. :abort gives up immediately (or
when the on_error hook says to stop) and fails the whole database.

A batch that cannot be saved is quarantined: its committed in-memory values
remain readable, the failure is recorded with the objects and pending writes it
contained, and unrelated reads and writes continue.db = create_database(DatabaseConfig(; dbname = "airdb_test", user = "airdb",

AirDB.sync(db)                   # does not throw

failed(db, vf.id)                # true — its row was not written

A quarantined batch is recorded, not lost: write_failures(db) lists the
records, failed(db, id) says whether one object is affected, and
clear_write_failure! acknowledges or retries it. Read errors are recorded
separately with read_failures. The whole inspection and retry API is in

With failure = :abort, the first permanent failure fails the whole
database: db.failure is set, every later write raises, and every later read
raises. Nothing is silently lost, but the database is unusable until it is
replaced.cfg = DatabaseConfig(; dbname = "airdb_test", user = "airdb",
                      password = "airdb", failure = :abort)

:retry is a compatibility alias for the isolated retry path: a failed
operation is retried, reconnecting first, while a budget lasts. Reads block
until a retry succeeds (or the budget is spent); writes accumulate in the
pipeline meanwhile. When the budget is spent the batch is quarantined, as under
:isolate.cfg = DatabaseConfig(;
    dbname     = "airdb_test",
    user       = "airdb",
    password   = "airdb",
    failure    = :retry,
    retries    = 5,          # retry at most 5 times ...
    retry_time = 30.0,       # ... or for at most 30 seconds (whichever first)
    retry_delay = 0.1,       # wait 0.1 s before the first retry ...
    retry_delay_max = 5.0,   # ... doubling up to 5 s between attempts
)

vf = VolatileForm(db, n = 1)
AirDB.sync(db)
close(AirDB._writer_conn(db))    # test-only: force an outage (internal helper)

AirDB.sync(db)                   # the writer reconnects, retries, and succeeds
vf[:n]                           # 2
db.failure === nothing           # true — the database is healthy

(retry_time), or both — whichever runs out first wins. If you set neither, a
small default is used.

Set on_error to a function on_error(db, err) and it is called on every
database error — writer or reader — before the policy is applied. Its return
value decides whether to retry:

return

meaning

outage, every read independently retries for up to retry_time before failing,
and the pipeline’s queue keeps growing until it recovers or gives up.

Rows accumulate for objects that nothing refers to any more: an unnamed form,
an actor that finished, a promise whose referrer is gone — delivered or not,

The roots are:

every name in form_name (see

and

every live in-memory object — a

ActorForm, 

PromiseForm,


StreamForm, or extern handle — that is still reachable
in the process.

A name is a root forever unless you release it with
delete_name!(db, name).

Collection is conservative: an object still referenced anywhere in the
process is kept. That is always safe — gc! never removes something in use —
but a just-released object may survive one sweep.

Links are found by a structural scan of the stored JSON. Every link string begins
with a marker (@, !, ~, &, or an {"extern": …} object), while user
strings begin with ' and symbols with :, so the scan cannot mistake data for
a link (see

would reject — a malformed marker — is not a link the sweep can resolve, so such
a row is left alone rather than being read as reachable.

committed values to reach the write pipeline. Air guarantees that a message sent
during a transaction is dispatched only if the transaction commits, and in
commit order. So the database sees exactly the transactions that succeeded, in

sync message every earlier write is on disk.@tx widget[:n] = 42

queued and saved asynchronously. sync is for tests, shutdown, and the moments
when another process — or a later session — must see the write.

the writer has not yet reached PostgreSQL: the form is cached in memory and the
pending write keeps it alive.@tx widget[:n] = 43

A project usually has a few well-known forms — a "root" holding shared
data, a "settings" form, a per-user entry point. Rather than pass UUIDs
around, give a form a name.

A name is just an alias: it lives in a form_name table, and the form it
points to still has its own UUID and its own rows in form_history and
form_current. The table is small, so a Database keeps it in memory as a
PDict{String,VolatileForm} — Air’s immutable dictionary — and, because names
are almost always changed inside a transaction, that PDict lives in an Air
Volatile. A change to it is therefore transactional: it commits with the
surrounding transaction and is retried or discarded with it, like any other
write. See 

Transactions.

records.content:
named_form looks a name up. A name may be a Symbol or a String — both refer
to the same form, because a name is compared by its string value.

create decides what happens when the name is not found:

create

name found

name not found

false (the default)

return the form

raise

true

raise

create a new named form and return it

nothing

return the form

return nothingusing AirDB

named_form(db, "root")                    # ERROR if "root" is not registered
named_form(db, "root"; create = nothing)  # nothing if it is not registered
named_form(db, :root; create = nothing)   # Symbol and String agree

With create = true, a new form is created and registered when the name is
free:root = named_form(db, "root"; create = true, value = form(version = 1))
named_form(db, "root") === root         # true
named_form(db, "root"; create = true)   # ERROR: the name "root" is already in use

The value argument is the new form’s initial value, used only when a form is
created. It may be:

a Form — used as-is;

anything a form can be made from, such as a number — converted, so 5 becomes
Form(5);

no value (the default) — an empty container;

an existing VolatileForm — in which case no new form is made, and the
name is simply pointed at the given form.named_form(db, "a"; create = true, value = form(x = 1))  # holds Form(x=1)
named_form(db, "b"; create = true, value = 5)            # holds Form(5)
named_form(db, "c"; create = true)                       # holds an empty container

shared = VolatileForm(db, n = 1)
named_form(db, "d"; create = true, value = shared)       # aliases `shared`
named_form(db, "d") === shared                           # true — the same object

name_form! registers a form under a name, overwriting whatever was there;
delete_name! releases the name:name_form!(db, "current", some_form)
name_form!(db, "current", another_form)   # now points at another_form
delete_name!(db, "current")               # the name is free again

Deleting a name does not delete the form; the form keeps its rows and can be
reached by its UUID.

named_forms returns the whole table as a PDict{String,VolatileForm}. A PDict
is immutable, so the result is safe to share and to keep; each value is a
(possibly not-yet-loaded) VolatileForm.names = named_forms(db)
names["root"]           # the form named "root"
haskey(names, "settings")

The table is loaded when a database is opened, so another process — or a later
session — finds the same names.close(db)
db = open_database(cfg)
value(named_form(db, "root")[:version])   # 1

The name table is a Volatile, so registering, renaming, or deleting a name is
transactional. named_form with create = true and name_form! join the
caller’s transaction if there is one, and otherwise run in a transaction of
their own — so you can call them anywhere.@tx begin
    root = named_form(db, "root"; create = true, value = form(version = 1))
    root[:version] = 2                  # both commit together
end

and the change is discarded if the transaction does not commit:try
    @tx begin
        named_form(db, "temp"; create = true)
        error("abort")
    end
catch
end
named_form(db, "temp"; create = nothing)   # nothing — the registration never happened

Reading the table inside a transaction registers a read of it, so a transaction
that looks a name up is retried if another transaction changes the table — the
same optimistic rule as every other write. See 

Transactions.

AirDB keeps an append-only history and an up-to-date snapshot of forms, plus the
tables for named forms and the live-object kinds introduced later. This page
covers the core form tables; each live kind’s table is described on its page.

CREATE TABLE form_history (
    form_id     UUID        NOT NULL,
    version     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
    tx_id       BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    payload     JSONB       NOT NULL,
    metadata    JSONB,
    PRIMARY KEY (form_id, version)
);

CREATE TABLE form_current (
    form_id     UUID        PRIMARY KEY,
    version     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
    payload     JSONB       NOT NULL,
    metadata    JSONB,
    history     BOOLEAN     NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE
);

-- The alias table for named forms (see Named forms).
CREATE TABLE form_name (
    name        TEXT        PRIMARY KEY,
    form_id     UUID        NOT NULL REFERENCES form_current(form_id)
);

Every committed update appends a new row to form_history and upserts
form_current, in one database transaction. Reads fetch exclusively from
form_current, so a lookup is an indexed point read by form_id. The version
is assigned by the database (1 on the first insert, one more each time), and
tx_id groups the rows written by a single commit.db = create_database(cfg; overwrite = true)
vf = VolatileForm(db, "widget", n = 1)
AirDB.sync(db)

@tx vf[:n] = 2
AirDB.sync(db)
# form_current:  version = 2
# form_history:  (version 1, tx_id 1), (version 2, tx_id 2)

A form created with history = false skips the history row: its current row is
overwritten in place. The choice is fixed when the form is created:vf = VolatileForm(db, n = 1; history = false)

A 

promise, 

actor, and

pages give the details.

AirDB’s writes go through Air’s software transactional memory. This page explains
the transaction model from scratch; the database side — how a commit becomes a
durable write — is the next page,


Commits and durability.

A VolatileForm is a thin wrapper around an Air Volatile{Form}. It can be read
at any time, but it may only be written inside a transaction:using AirDB, Air

widget = VolatileForm(db, "widget", n = 1)

@tx widget[:n] = 42       # stage the change ...
# ... it commits here, and the writer is told to save the new form
value(widget[:n])          # 42

Outside a transaction a write is an error, inherited from Air:widget[:n] = 5
# ERROR: cannot set volatile outside of transaction

The tx function is the non-macro form, handy when you already have a closure:tx(() -> (widget[:n] = value(widget[:n]) + 1))

All the writes in one transaction become visible together, and all the sends are
dispatched together, in commit order. A commit that changes several forms writes
them to the database in a single database transaction, so a reader never sees
half of a commit.a = VolatileForm(db, kind = "A")
b = VolatileForm(db, kind = "B")

@tx begin
    a[:v] = 1
    b[:v] = 2
end
AirDB.sync(db)
(value(a[:v]), value(b[:v]))   # (1, 2) — both landed together

The body may run more than once

records.content:
Air is optimistic: a transaction records what it reads, and if any of those
values change before it commits, the transaction is discarded and re-run. So the
body of a transaction must be free of side effects other than the transactional
ones.# Good: the only side effect is the transactional write.
@tx widget[:n] = value(widget[:n]) + 1

# Bad: this prints a different number of times depending on contention.
@tx begin
    println("attempt")          # do not do this
    widget[:n] = value(widget[:n]) + 1
end

If the body throws, nothing is written:try
    @tx begin
        widget[:n] = 99
        error("abort")
    end
catch
end
value(widget[:n])                 # still 42 — the write never happened

Reading a form inside a transaction registers an Air read, so the transaction
sees a consistent value and will be re-run if it changes. A form that has not
yet been loaded from the database is loaded on first access; that is ordinary
lazy loading (see


Lazy loading and the cache), and it is safe inside
a transaction.@tx begin
    current = value(widget[:n])   # read (and register)
    widget[:n] = current + 1      # write
end

Within one process, a read always sees the latest committed value even if the
database writer has not caught up: the live form is cached in memory. Making a
write durable — waiting until PostgreSQL has it — is the subject of
